First, the in vitro design, conducted using phantom heads, was chosen to restrict operator access and standardize conditions. However, this approach does not fully replicate the clinical challenges and complexities encountered in real patients. The implants in the study herein did not have implant restorations present, and all the implants were affected by a 5 mm horizontal implant defect with no adjacent teeth. This limits the generalizability of our study to cases which may have those factors present in clinical practice. It has already been shown that the presence of a crown can result in increased residual threads in a phantom head study with a soft tissue model present (Burgueño‐Barris et al. ). A single operator performed IP of all implants in our study. Although a sole operator was used to limit inter‐operator variability, this also reduces the generalizability of the results. Individual operator skill and technique vary, with some clinicians potentially being able to achieve improved results. In addition, the application of pressure was not controlled for when performing IP on the dental implants on the phantom head and tabletop models. In this way, it was attempted to reproduce the real‐world conditions present in a patient's mouth. However, this lack of pressure control means that our outcomes, while generally repeatable by the same operator, might differ if another operator performs the procedure. Future research should investigate how the presence of different morphologies of peri‐implant defects, the presence of implant restoration, and the use of a soft tissue model would affect outcomes of IP. 5 Conclusion Implants treated with IP in the phantom‐head set‐up exhibited significantly greater surface roughness and required a longer time compared to those treated in the table‐top model, but did not influence material loss. The increased duration is likely due to the added complexity and restricted access inherent in a simulated intraoral environment, as opposed to the freer table‐top set‐up. OSCC is characterised by insidious onset, aggressive local invasion, and a high rate of cervical lymph node metastasis, posing a significant threat to human health and quality of life. Notably, between 20% and 60% of OSCC cases arise from oral potentially malignant disorders (OPMDs). Among these, oral leukoplakia (OLK) is the most common, defined as a predominantly white plaque of questionable risk, having excluded (other) known diseases or disorders that carry no increased risk for cancer. The global prevalence of OLK is estimated at 3.41%, with a reported malignant transformation rate of 6.64%. Therefore, early identification and intervention targeting key factors influencing the malignant transformation of OLK, along with the development of effective risk prediction tools, are critical for reducing the incidence of OSCC. Several clinicopathological and behavioural risk factors for OLK malignant transformation have been well established, including age, sex, smoking and betel-quid use, lesion location, lesion size, clinical subtype and the severity of oral epithelial dysplasia (OED). , , , The latest meta-analysis further confirmed that OED, nonhomogeneous leukoplakia, larger lesion size, location at the lingual margin and smoking are the factors strongly associated with OLK malignant transformation. However, most studies have focused on the general OLK populations, while patients with comorbid systemic diseases, particularly those with type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM), have received limited attention. T2DM is one of the most prevalent chronic metabolic diseases worldwide, associated with microvascular and macrovascular complications. Increasing evidence indicates that T2DM contributes to the development of multiple solid tumours, including colorectal, breast and pancreatic cancers. , And its potential role in head and neck cancers, including OSCC, has attracted growing interest. Meta-analyses have suggested that individuals with T2DM have an elevated risk of developing oral cancer (RR = 1.15). Moreover, higher prevalence of OPMDs, particularly OLK and oral lichen planus (OLP), has been reported among individuals with T2DM or chronic hyperglycemia, , , , , , suggesting a potential metabolic link. Our previous research revealed that hyperglycaemia markedly increases the risk of OLK malignant transformation (aHR = 4.7), and proliferative verrucous leukoplakia patients with T2DM were more prone to malignant progression. These findings raise the critical question of whether glycaemic control – an essential element of diabetes management – modifies malignant risk in OLK patients. Mechanistically, poor glycaemic control may promote carcinogenesis through inflammation, oxidative stress and immune suppression. , , , Although recent OLK predictive models have incorporated diabetes as a significant prognostic variable, none have specifically addressed the role of glycaemic control in OLK-T2DM patients. Predictive models to identify high-risk OLK-T2DM patients are still lacking. To address this gap, we conducted a nested case–control study. Patients were selected from a real-world cohort of OLK-T2DM patients at Peking University School and Hospital of Stomatology since January 2013 and were prospectively followed until March 2025 to monitor malignant transformation with a minimum follow-up period of 6 months. Based on the follow-up outcomes, patients who developed malignant transformation into OSCC were defined as the case group, whereas those without malignant transformation were designated as the control group. This study aimed to identify clinicopathological and metabolic factors associated with malignant transformation in OLK-T2DM patients, with a particular focus on glycaemic control. Furthermore, predictive models based on glycaemic indicators were developed to identify malignant transformation risk in OLK-T2DM patients. This study provides new evidence to inform risk stratification and targeted prevention strategies in this high-risk group. Multivariate conditional logistic regression analysis Multivariable conditional logistic regression analysis was conducted to evaluate the independent effects of FPG and other risk factors on the malignant transformation of OLK. The models were conditioned on the matching variables (age and sex). Adjustment and interaction variables were selected based on a comprehensive literature review and the construction of a directed acyclic graph ( ). Four hierarchical models were established. The first was the Minimally Adjusted Model, which included only the matching variables (age and sex) and examined FPG (continuous) as the main predictors. The second model, called the Lifestyle-Adjusted Model, was built upon Model 1 by further adjusting for lifestyle-related factors, including tobacco use and alcohol consumption. The third model, known as the Clinically-Adjusted Model, added adjustments for clinical characteristics of OLK, including the initial grade of OED, lesion location (tongue vs nontongue), and OLK duration (continuous variable), in addition to the variables included in Model 2. Finally, the Fully Adjusted Model (Model 4) incorporated additional covariates, including lesion size (continuous variable), the presence of other systemic diseases (yes/no), and personal history of malignancy, in addition to the variables in Model 3. Multivariable stratified Cox regression models We employed stratified Cox proportional hazards regression models to estimate adjusted hazard ratios (aHR) with 95% CI, accounting for the 1:2 age- and sex-matched design to provide more appropriate estimates than a standard Cox model. The model-building procedure was similar to that of multivariate conditional logistic regression, except that Model 4 excluded personal history of malignancy due to an extremely sparse number of outcome events in this category, which would otherwise result in complete separation and infinite parameter estimates if this variable were forcibly included in the model. Univariate and multivariate analyses were compared to evaluate key risk factors for OLK malignant transformation. Handling of missing data Initially, missing data were handled using pairwise deletion: for each univariable analysis, cases with missing values for the variable of interest were excluded from that analysis only. Multivariable conditional logistic regression models were restricted to patients with complete data for all included covariates. Subsequently, missing data were handled using multiple imputation by chained equations (m = 10) to retain the full sample size for the multivariable stratified Cox regression analyses. All relevant variables were included in the imputation model. The final estimates and standard errors were pooled according to Rubin’s rules to appropriately account for uncertainty due to missing data. The matched design was preserved throughout the imputation and analysis process, and stratified Cox models with a strata term were used to account for the 1:2 matched sets. No significant differences in sex or age distribution were observed ( P > .05). The baseline demographic and clinical, and lifestyle characteristics were summarised in . Clinical characteristics The clinical lesion type did not differ significantly. The median lesion size was significantly larger in the cases than in the controls. Lesions located on the tongue were significantly associated with malignant transformation (OR = 2.71, P = .005). Pathological grading of OED revealed a stepwise increase in cancer risk with increasing severity. Compared to simple epithelial hyperplasia, mild, moderate and severe OED had ORs of 4.31 ( P = .003), 13.50 ( P < .001) and 9.21 ( P = .001), respectively. In addition, longer OLK duration was significantly associated with malignant transformation (OR = 1.01 per month, P = .013) ( ). Glycaemic control and diabetes-related indicators The median FPG level was significantly higher in the cases compared to the controls [9.5 (8.0, 11.0) mmol/L vs 7.0 (6.0, 8.5) mmol/L; OR = 1.76, P < .001], indicating a positive association between elevated FPG levels and malignant transformation in OLK-T2DM patients. The high proportion of missing values of HbA1c (75.76%) limited statistical comparison, and no significant difference was observed. Furthermore, patients were further categorised as optimal or suboptimal glycaemic control. A significantly greater proportion of cases exhibited suboptimal glycaemic control compared with controls (70.9% vs 37.3%; P < .001). In univariate conditional logistic regression, suboptimal glycaemic control remained independently associated with malignant transformation (OR = 4.10, P < .001). The median duration of T2DM did not differ significantly, indicating that T2DM duration alone was not associated with malignant transformation in this cohort ( ). Lifestyle factors, comorbidities, and family history No significant difference was observed in lifestyle-related factors, including tobacco use, alcohol consumption and betel-quid use (all P > .05). Likewise, individual comorbidities such as hypertension and hyperlipidaemia were not significantly associated with malignant transformation. However, patients without any other relevant systemic diseases beyond T2DM showed a significantly lower risk (OR = 0.35, P = .013), suggesting that overall systemic health status may play a protective role. A family history of malignancy was more frequent in the cases (5.5%) compared with none in the controls ( P = .036), indicating a potential genetic or hereditary predisposition among the cases ( ). Dose–response relationship No significant association was observed across different durations of T2DM. In contrast, longer duration of OLK was associated with a stepwise increase in malignant transformation risk ( P = .001). Patients with a lesion size greater than 200 mm 2 had a significantly higher risk compared with those with smaller lesions (≤ 200 mm 2 , P = .007). However, no significant statistical differences were detected across different categories of smoking index or alcohol consumption ( ). Among other covariates, moderate OED remained significantly associated with malignant transformation (aOR = 22.46, P = .011) ( ). Multivariable stratified Cox regression models Multivariable stratified Cox regression models revealed that FPG was significantly associated with malignant transformation in all models. The aHRs for FPG were 1.60 ( P = .013), 1.62 ( P = .010) and 2.23 ( P = .015) for Models 1, 2 and 3, respectively and 2.74 ( P = .032) for Model 4. In Models 3 and 4, moderate and severe OED were independently associated with malignant transformation (aHR = 96.62; P = .006; aHR = 399.43; P = .021, respectively) . FPG remained a significant independent predictor in all models: for every 1 mmol/L increase in FPG, the risk of malignant transformation increased by 60% to 174% ( ). A comparison of key risk factors for malignant transformation in OLK based on univariate and 2 types of multivariate analyses is presented in . Multivariate clinical prediction model Among the 3 machine learning algorithms, the Random Forest achieved the best overall performance, with an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) of 0.78 ± 0.12 (95% CI: 0.71-0.85, P < .001) representing acceptable predictive performance. The calibration plot for the Random Forest model indicates that the predicted probabilities were generally consistent with the actual outcome fractions ( ). The AUC of Linear SVM and LASSO were 0.72 ± 0.13 (95% CI: 0.64-0.81, P < .001) and 0.65 ± 0.09 (95% CI: 0.56–0.75, P = .001), respectively ( A-C). The Linear SVM yielded the highest classification accuracy (76.91% ± 12.30) and F-measure (0.83 ± 0.10), indicating stable ability in identifying malignant transformation cases ( ). Feature importance ranking based on information gain identified FPG as the most informative variable, followed by simple epithelial hyperplasia (Grade = 0), moderate OED (Grade = 2), lesion location on the tongue, the presence of other systemic diseases and severe OED (Grade = 3). Only features with an information gain score > .01 were included ( D). To comprehensively evaluate feature importance, the distinct interpretability mechanisms of 3 machine learning models: Random forest, LASSO logistic regression, and linear SVM were leveraged. FPG consistently emerged as the single most important predictor across all 3 models (Random forest importance = 0.36; SVM coefficient = 5.36; LASSO coefficient = 3.84). OED grade was validated as a critical stratification factor ( ). In conclusion, the 3 models are consistent with the information gain results. FPG is the most core predictor of malignant transformation risk of OLK-T2DM patients. Discussion The malignant transformation of OLK represents a persistent clinical challenge, and T2DM has increasingly been recognised as a systemic disease closely associated with various oral conditions, including periodontal disease, dental caries and OPMDs, , , and associated with heightened cancer susceptibility. However, risk factors for malignant transformation in OLK-T2DM patients remain largely undefined. Most previous studies have focused on general OLK populations, emphasising demographic, behavioural and lesion-related characteristics, , whereas metabolic risk profiles in OLK-T2DM patients have received limited attention. In this nested case–control study based on the real-world cohort of OLK-T2DM patients, we demonstrated that suboptimal glycaemic control was strongly and independently associated with increased risk of malignant transformation. Each 1 mmol/L increase in FPG raised malignant transformation risk by 60% to 174%. In addition, a higher initial OED grade was confirmed as an independent predictor, whereas clinical lesion type, T2DM duration, tobacco use, alcohol consumption and betel-quid use were not significantly associated. Notably, the consistency between the results of logistic regression and Cox proportional hazards models further supports the robustness of our findings and underscores the importance of accounting for the time-to-event nature of malignant transformation. Building on these findings, we developed multifactorial prediction models that integrated glycaemic and key clinical indicators. Across all models, FPG consistently ranked as the most important predictor, reinforcing its central role in malignant transformation risk. Notably, the Linear SVM model achieved a cross-validated accuracy of 76.91%, suggesting the feasibility of translating this approach into a clinically applicable risk scoring tool. Such a tool may facilitate early identification of high-risk patients, guide individualised follow-up, and support shared decision-making to reduce malignant transformation and improve long-term outcomes. This study developed a multifactorial risk prediction model specifically for the OLK-T2DM population. The model remains exploratory and is intended primarily as a primary clinical screening tool rather than a replacement for precision diagnostics. Although some specialised AI models integrating pathomics or molecular features have reported higher discriminative performance with AUCs ranging from 0.88 to 0.96, they differ substantially from our model. , , Existing models generally focus on the general OLK cohort, whereas our model is the first specifically designed for OLK-T2DM comorbidity populations. In addition, high-performance models typically require advanced pathological infrastructure, such as whole-slide digital scanning, immunohistochemical platforms and molecular testing laboratories, whereas our model relies solely on routine clinical variables (e.g., FPG, lesion characteristics). Consequently, while specialised models may achieve higher AUCs, their clinical applicability is often limited to tertiary medical centres with comprehensive resources. In contrast, our model can facilitate rapid risk stratification in primary care or resource-limited settings by using widely available clinical data. Despite the lower discriminative performance compared with specialised models, our model highlights the potential of clinical-only prediction tools for early identification of high-risk patients, and future improvements may include more comprehensive integration of pathological or multi-omics features as well as validation in larger, independent cohorts. A meta-analysis further reported a 15% increased risk of oral cancer in patients with T2DM. And Yen et al reported a 35% increase in all-cause mortality in OLK-T2DM. Subsequent studies have demonstrated that prediabetes and diabetes are closely linked to an increased risk of OLP. , , In 2010, a cross-sectional study by Saini et al revealed that OLP lesions in diabetic patients exhibit higher malignancy potential compared to those in non-diabetic individuals. More recently, a prospective cohort study by Kamal et al in 2024 found that OLP patients with diabetes had lower levels of salivary antioxidant levels than those without diabetes, suggesting that oxidative stress may play a potential role in the malignant transformation of OLP with diabetes. In conclusion, diabetes is not only a comorbidity but also increases the prevalence and malignant transformation risk of OPMDs. The molecular mechanisms by which hyperglycaemia promotes the progression of OLK to OSCC are not fully elucidated, but several experimental findings provide plausible pathways. Hyperglycaemia may facilitate the malignant transformation of OLK to OSCC through the activation of the epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR) signalling pathway and subsequent glycolytic reprogramming. The underlying mechanisms involve enhanced cellular proliferation, migration and increased glucose uptake – potentially mediated by glucose transporter 1 (GLUT1). These processes collectively promote a malignant phenotype. However, further in vivo studies are required to validate these mechanisms and their potential synergistic contributions to OSCC progression. , , , , , This study is novel in its relatively large hospital-based cohort of OLK-T2DM patients and the use of a nested case–control design, which minimised bias and enhanced validity. Nevertheless, several limitations should be mentioned. First, the retrospective design means that some clinical information was not available for all patients, particularly HbA1c. A major reason for the high missing rate of HbA1c is that it was not formally included in the Chinese diagnostic criteria for diabetes until the release of the Guideline for the prevention and treatment of type 2 diabetes mellitus in China (2020 edition) in April 2021, where HbA1c ≥ 6.5% was introduced as a supplementary diagnostic criterion. During most of the study period (2013–2025), FPG, random blood glucose, or OGTT 2-hour glucose remained the primary diagnostic indicators in routine clinical practice and HbA1c testing was not consistently performed. Consequently, the use of HbA1c in statistical analysis was limited. In the present study, the classification of glycaemic control did not rely solely on HbA1c. According to the 2025 ADA and the Chinese Guidelines for the Prevention and Treatment of T2DM (2024), FPG was used when HbA1c data were unavailable, with optimal control defined as 4.4 to 7.2 mmol/L and suboptimal control as >7.2 mmol/L. In future prospective studies, comprehensive HbA1c data collection is warranted to enhance the robustness of study findings. Second, the models developed in this study lack external validation and were derived from a single-centre cohort, which may limit their generalisability. Therefore, these models should be considered exploratory and require validation in independent, prospective cohorts before any clinical application. Furthermore, future optimisation of the model will focus on developing advanced versions that integrate pathomics features (e.g., KRT13, Ki-67, p53) with multi-omics data. , Third, a limitation of this study is the relatively short minimum follow-up period of 6 months. This duration may limit the total number of observable malignant transformation events and could lead to an underestimation of the overall transformation rate, thereby affecting the assessment of long-term risk. However, as a nested case-control study, our primary aim was to evaluate associations between clinicopathological and metabolic risk factors and malignant transformation rather than to estimate absolute transformation rates. Future prospective studies with longer follow-up are warranted to more accurately assess the lifetime risk of malignant transformation in patients with OLK. Fourth, the biological mechanisms linking hyperglycaemia to malignant transformation remain to be fully elucidated. Overall, these limitations should be addressed in future studies, which require independent validation in larger, prospective cohorts before they can be considered for clinical use. Conclusion This nested case–control study demonstrated that suboptimal glycaemic control (HbA1c > 7% or FPG > 7.2 mmol/L) was a strong and independent predictor of malignant transformation in OLK-T2DM patients. Elevated FPG, together with OED grade, consistently increased risk across both regression and machine learning models. Future clinical practice should move beyond managing OLK and T2DM in isolation. Actively incorporate assessment and optimisation of glycaemic status (e.g., FPG levels) as a core component of the standard care plan for OLK-T2DM patients. Management should aim for strict glycaemic targets to reduce potentially malignant transformation risk. chunks.content: 1. Introduction Non-communicable diseases (NCDs) are rising in prevalence globally in line with an increasingly ageing population, refined diets and sedentary lifestyles. NCDs account for 41 million deaths each year, or 71% of all global deaths [ ]. Approximately 80% of people over the age of 65 in the USA are affected by one or more NCDs, and 77% exhibit at least two NCDs, creating a significant burden of disease to individuals and to the healthcare economy [ ]. The co-morbid presence of two or more NCDs presents a major challenge to the economy, equating to two thirds of all health costs in the USA [ ]; however, less than 1% of health expenditure in the USA is focussed on prevention to improve overall health [ ]. The greatest global NCD burden arises due to cardiovascular disease (CVD), which is responsible for 17.9 million deaths (one third of total mortality) and 45% of NCD-induced mortality [ ]. In Europe, CVD is responsible for 3.9 million deaths (45% of deaths), and whilst CVD mortality rates are reducing, the absolute numbers have increased in the last 25 years due to an increasingly ageing population [ ]. Ischaemic heart disease, stroke, hypertension (leading to heart failure), rheumatic heart disease, cardiomyopathy and atrial fibrillation cause over 95% of CVD-related deaths [ ]. In this consensus report, the term CVD is used as a general term for atherosclerotic diseases, principally coronary heart disease, cerebrovascular disease and peripheral vascular disease. A number of chronic infectious-inflammatory-immune diseases are associated with significantly higher risks of adverse cardiovascular events, including rheumatoid arthritis, psoriasis, systemic lupus erythematosus and periodontitis [ ], consistent with the thesis that chronic elevations in the systemic inflammatory burden are causally related to CVD development and its sequelae. Whilst there is evidence for over 50 gene polymorphisms playing a role in the modulation of atherogenesis [ ], effect sizes are small and the major traditional risk factors for CVD remain lifestyle factors, principally tobacco smoking, dyslipidaemia, hypertension and altered glucose metabolism. The latter correlate strongly with diets high in saturated fats, salt and refined sugars and contribute to obesity and type 2 diabetes mellitus, major attributable risk factors for myocardial infarction [ ]. The same risk factors account for over 90% of the stroke burden [ ], yet all are modifiable through improved lifestyles, including reducing salt, saturated fat and refined carbohydrate intake, exercising, increasing intake of antioxidant micronutrients and regular moderate alcohol consumption [ ]. Periodontitis is also an NCD with a high prevalence of 45–50% overall, with the most severe form affecting 11.2% of the world’s population, making it the sixth most common human disease [ ]. The Global Burden of Diseases, Injuries, and Risk Factors Study (2017) of Years Lost to Disability (YLD) reported that from 1990 to 2017 oral diseases (mainly periodontitis and caries) contributed the most YLD in age-standardised prevalence rates from 354 diseases and injuries across 195 countries [ ]. There is now a significant body of evidence to support independent associations between severe periodontitis and several NCDs, including diabetes [ ], cardiovascular disease [ ], chronic obstructive pulmonary disease [ ] and chronic kidney disease (CKD) [ ]. Indeed, severe periodontitis is independently and significantly associated with all-cause and cardiovascular mortality in several different populations [ ]. Proposed mechanisms include bacteraemia and the associated systemic inflammatory sequelae, including elevations in C-reactive protein and oxidative stress [ ]. In populations with multi-morbidity, for example chronic kidney disease with co-morbid diabetes and periodontitis, periodontitis is associated with significantly reduced survival from all-cause and cardiovascular mortality [ ]. It appears, therefore, that periodontitis may be a modifiable non-traditional risk factor for CVD. In 2012 a joint workshop was held between the European Federation of Periodontology (EFP) and the American Academy of Periodontology to review the literature relating periodontitis and systemic diseases, including CVD. The consensus report was based upon four technical papers that systematically reviewed the evidence for epidemiological associations between periodontitis and incident CVD [ ], mechanisms of biological plausibility relating to periodontal bacteria and systemic inflammation [ ] and periodontal intervention studies [ ]. The workshop concluded there was consistent and strong epidemiological evidence that periodontitis imparts increased risk for future atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease. It also concluded the impact of periodontitis on CVD was biologically plausible, via translocated circulating oral microbiota, which may directly or indirectly induce systemic inflammation that impacts upon the development of atherothrombogenesis, and whilst in vitro, pre-clinical and clinical studies supported the interaction and associated biological mechanisms, intervention trials were not sufficiently adequate to draw further conclusions at that time. The present workshop was jointly organised by the EFP and the World Heart Federation (WHF) to include global experts in both periodontal and cardiovascular disciplines and was held in Madrid on 18 and 19 February 2019.

Four technical reviews updating the evidence base from the 2012 workshop were prepared and supplemented by additional studies discussed at the workshop. The reviews focussed on epidemiological associations [ ], mechanistic links [ ], results from intervention studies [ ] and the potential risk and complications of periodontal therapy in patients undertaking antithrombotic (antiplatelet and anticoagulant) therapy. While this consensus report focuses predominantly on relevant evidence published since the 2012 workshop, there are biological areas that have subsequently come to prominence, and where the underpinning body of evidence was not covered in the 2013 consensus report; hence, certain pre-2012 manuscripts are referenced to ensure the context of these recent studies is clear. Furthermore, sections 4.3: What is the effect of statin intake on clinical periodontal outcomes? and section 5: Cardiovascular risks and complications of periodontal therapeutic interventions were not dealt with in the previous workshop; hence, a full appraisal of the scientific evidence was carried out in this consensus meeting. Finally, following the review of the presented evidence, recommendations for both medical and dental teams, as well as patients and the public, were elaborated. 2. Epidemiologic evidence on the association between periodontitis and CVD 2.1. Do people with periodontitis have a higher prevalence of subclinical cardiovascular disease? There is evidence from epidemiological studies that periodontitis patients exhibit significant endothelial dysfunction, measured by flow mediated dilation (FMD), arterial stiffness (e.g., pulse wave velocity – PWV) and a significantly greater thickness of the carotid intima media (cIMT) and elevated arterial calcification scores. There is one imaging study (ATHEROREMO-IVUS study) associating high levels of antibodies against periodontal pathogens and a lower extent of positive atheromatous plaque remodelling [ ]. 2.2. Do people with periodontitis have a higher prevalence of coronary artery disease and risk of myocardial infarction and other coronary events? There is robust evidence from epidemiological studies for a positive association between periodontitis and coronary heart disease. A systematic review [ ], which was updated in preparation for this workshop, identified a total of six case-control and cohort epidemiological studies, published in the last five years, which demonstrated an increased risk of a first coronary event in patients with clinically diagnosed periodontitis or more severe periodontitis compared to patients without periodontitis or less severe periodontitis. Relative risk estimates vary between studies, depending on population characteristics and periodontitis case definitions. There are two cohort studies reporting an association between periodontitis and higher cardiovascular mortality (due to coronary heart disease and cerebrovascular disease). 2.3. Do people with periodontitis have a higher prevalence of cerebrovascular disease and risk of stroke? There is evidence from epidemiologic studies for a positive association between periodontitis and cerebrovascular disease. A systematic review [ ], which was updated in preparation for this workshop, identified a total of three case-control and cohort studies, which demonstrate an increased risk of a first cerebrovascular event in patients with clinically diagnosed periodontitis or more severe periodontitis compared to patients without periodontitis or less severe periodontitis. Relative risk estimates vary between studies, depending on population characteristics and periodontitis case definitions. Furthermore, a recent analysis of data from the Atherosclerosis Risk in Communities (ARIC) study demonstrated an association between periodontal profile class and incident ischemic stroke. In this cohort, patients with periodontitis had more than double the risk of cardioembolic and thrombotic stroke compared to periodontally healthy individuals [ ]. In addition, as previously documented, there are two cohort studies reporting an association between periodontitis and higher cardiovascular mortality (due to coronary heart disease and cerebrovascular disease) [ ]. 2.4. Do people with periodontitis have a higher prevalence and incidence of Peripheral Artery Disease (PAD)? There is limited but consistent evidence that individuals with periodontitis have a higher prevalence and incidence of PAD compared to individuals without periodontitis [ ]. For cross-sectional data, the most significant evidence comes from two large, population-based studies in the USA (NHANES 1999–2002) and South Korea (KoGES-CAVAS). Do people with periodontitis have a higher risk of other CVDs or conditions (heart failure, atrial fibrillation)? Several studies report positive associations between periodontitis and heart failure. Do people with a history of cardiovascular disease have a different incidence or progression of periodontitis? There is currently limited scientific evidence that CVD is a risk factor for the onset or progression of periodontitis. 2.7. Do people with periodontitis with history of cardiovascular disease have a higher chance of experiencing a subsequent event? From three studies investigating the association between periodontitis and secondary cardiovascular events, two large studies did not find a significant association [ ]; however, a small study (100 subjects) reported a significant association (HR = 2.8, 95% CI [1.2; 6.5]) with recurrent cerebro-vascular events [ ]. 3. Mechanisms that may explain the epidemiological associations between periodontitis and CVD 3.1. Is there evidence of a higher incidence of bacteremia following oral function/intervention in periodontitis patients compared to periodontally healthy subjects? There is evidence that oral bacterial species can enter the circulation and cause bacteremia, which has been demonstrated following daily life activities (tooth brushing, flossing, chewing or biting an apple), although it has been studied more frequently following professional interventions (tooth polishing, scaling, tooth extraction, surgical extraction of third molars and periodontal probing). The risk of bacteremia has been associated with periodontal health status in a systematic review, suggesting a higher risk of bacteremia associated with gingival inflammation [ ]. A recent randomized clinical trial (RCT) concluded that periodontal therapy (by means of scaling and root planing, SRP) induced bacteremia in both gingivitis and periodontitis patients, but the magnitude and frequency were greater among periodontitis patients [ ]. Whilst there are methodological limitations in some of the reported studies, the overall picture supports the contention that bacteremia results from daily life activities and oral interventions, and it is more frequent, of longer duration and involves more virulent bacteria in periodontitis patients. 3.2. Is there evidence for the presence of oral bacteria in atheroma lesions? There is evidence through traces of DNA, RNA or antigens derived from oral bacterial species, mainly periodontal pathogens, that have been identified in atherothrombotic tissues. Studies have attempted to correlate the presence of these bacteria in atherothrombotic tissues with other sample sources (subgingival plaque, serum, etc.) in the same patients, and these suggest that in periodontitis patients there is a higher probability of a positive correlation [ ]. At least two studies have demonstrated viable P. gingivalis and A. actinomycetemcomitans in athero-thrombotic tissue when culturing the atheroma samples [ ]. 3.3. Do we have evidence that periodontal bacteria and/or bacterial products and virulence factors influence the pathophysiology of atherosclerosis? Different animal models have been employed to provide evidence that periodontal pathogens can promote atheroma formation. P. gingivalis has been shown to accelerate atherosclerosis in murine models, to induce fatty streaks in the aorta of rabbits and to induce aortic and coronary lesions after bacteremia in normocholesterolaemic pigs (Schenkein & Loos. 2003). Do we have evidence that periodontitis patients exhibit increased production and/or levels of inflammatory mediators also associated with the pathophysiology of atherosclerosis? There is evidence of significantly higher levels of C-reactive protein (CRP) in periodontitis patients versus healthy controls and in CVD and periodontitis patients compared with either condition alone. The effect of periodontal therapy has been shown to associate with a significant decrease in CRP levels, along with improvements in surrogate measurements of cardiovascular health [ , , ]. There is evidence of elevated levels of serum interleukin (IL)-6 in periodontitis patients and lower levels of IL-4 and IL-18. The effect of periodontal therapy has shown a significant decrease in the serum levels of IL-6, serum amyloid A and alpha 1 anti-chymotripsin. Peripheral neutrophils from periodontitis patients release excess IL-1β, IL-8, IL-6 and tumour necrosis factor (TNF)-α when stimulated by periodontal pathogens. Periodontal therapy only partially reduces the cytokine hyperreactivity with some evidence of a constitutively elevated response [ ]. 3.5. Do we have evidence that periodontitis patients develop elevations in thrombotic factors that are also associated with the pathophysiology of atherothrombosis? There is evidence of significantly higher levels of fibrinogen in periodontitis patients versus healthy controls and in CVD and periodontitis patients compared with either condition alone [ ]. Periodontal therapy appears to result in a significant decrease in fibrinogen levels [ ]. There is evidence from different studies of significantly higher levels of platelet activation markers in periodontitis patients and that these higher levels may be reversed by periodontal therapy [ ]. However, there is conflicting evidence that significantly higher levels of plasminogen activator inhibitor (PAI) are found in periodontitis patients (Schenkein & Loos. 2003). 3.6. Do we have evidence that periodontitis patients demonstrate elevated serum antibody levels that cross-react with antigens in cardiovascular tissues? There is evidence that Heat Shock Proteins (HSP) from periodontal pathogens ( Porphyromona gingivalis, Tannerella forsythia, Aggregatibacter actinomycetemcomitans and Fusobacterium nucleatum ) generate antibodies that can cross-react with human HSPs. These antibodies have been shown to activate cytokine production, as well as monocyte and endothelial cell activation. Presence of anti-cardiolipin antibodies have been significantly associated in periodontitis patients, which reversed following periodontal therapy. There is some evidence that periodontal pathogens can elicit antibodies that cross-react with cardiolipin (Schenkein & Loos. 2003). In three out of four population-based studies (Parogene study, NHANES III, DANHES), higher levels of serum immunoglobulin (Ig)G against P. gingivalis were associated with periodontitis patients and cardiovascular disease (acute coronary syndrome, death from cardiovascular disease and cardiovascular disease). The ATHEROREMO-IVUS study failed to demonstrate an association between serum levels of IgG and IgA against P. gingivalis, A. actinomycetemcomitans, T. forsythia and P. intermedia and major adverse cardiac events (MACE) [ ]. This is consistent with data from Boillot et al. [ ]. 3.7. Do we have evidence that periodontitis patients exhibit dyslipidemia? High-density lipoprotein (HDL) levels are reduced in periodontitis patients compared with controls (Schenkein & Loos. 2003). These levels are reversed after periodontal therapy [ ]. 3.8. Are there common genetic risk factors between periodontitis and CVDs? There is scientific evidence of pleiotropy between periodontitis and cardiovascular diseases [ , , , ]. The highly pleiotropic genetic locus CDKN2B-AS1 (chromosome 9, p21.3) associated with coronary artery disease, type 2 diabetes, ischemic stroke and Alzheimer’s disease is also consistently associated with periodontitis [ , , , ]. Its function appears to be related to the regulation of gene expression [ ]. Interestingly, a pilot study identified that a genetic variant in the CDKN2B-AS1 locus was associated with the extent of elevated levels of C-reactive protein in periodontitis [ ]. A conserved non-coding element within CAMTA1 upstream of VAMP3 , also first identified as a genetic susceptibility locus for coronary artery disease, was found to be associated with periodontitis [ ]. A GWAS suggested the VAMP3 locus was associated with a higher probability of subgingival overgrowth of periodontal pathogens [ ]. There is evidence for plasminogen (PLG) as a shared genetic risk factor for coronary artery disease and periodontitis [ ]. The fourth pleiotropic locus between coronary artery disease and periodontitis is a haplotype block at the VAMP8 locus [ ]. These shared genetic factors suggest a mechanistic link or immunological commonalities between coronary artery disease and periodontitis. The impairment of the regulatory pathways by genetic factors may be a common pathogenic denominator of at least coronary artery disease and periodontitis. There are indications that aberrant inflammatory reactivity, determined by genetic variants in the loci CDKN2B-AS1 (ANRIL), PLG, CAMTA1/VAMP3 and VAMP8 could partially explain the epidemiological link between periodontitis and cardiovascular diseases. 4. What is the effect of statin intake on clinical periodontal outcomes? Statins are medications prescribed to decrease LDL cholesterol. Numerous trials have demonstrated their benefit for the prevention of cardiovascular diseases [ ]. Interestingly, statins possess various additional properties relevant to the pathogenesis and treatment of periodontitis [ ]. In particular, it has been reported that statins are anti-inflammatory [ , , , , ], can promote bone formation [ , , , ], can inhibit matrix metalloproteinases (MMPs) [ , , ] and possess anti-microbial properties [ ]. Cardiovascular risks and complications of periodontal therapeutic interventions 5.1. Is there an ischemic cardiovascular risk for patients undergoing periodontal therapy? Non-surgical treatment of periodontitis involving supra- and sub-gingival instrumentation of the affected dentition (under local anaesthesia) is often delivered in several short sessions. Alternatively, full-mouth non-surgical periodontal treatment can be performed within 24 hours. Delivering periodontal treatment in a full-mouth fashion (i.e., within 24 hours) triggers a one-week acute systemic inflammatory response associated with a transient impairment of endothelial function [ ]. This distant effect is not observed when periodontal treatment is delivered across several separate sessions [ ]. This is achieved by limiting the number of teeth involved and the time devoted to completing the dental instrumentation. These findings raise the question of whether performing longer sessions of periodontal treatment could contribute to an individual’s inflammatory burden/risk and increase their short-term risk of suffering from a vascular event. There is consistent and strong observational evidence that common acute infections/inflammatory responses are associated at a population level with an increased risk of vascular events within the first four weeks of the infectious/inflammatory event [ ]. 5.1.1. At population level There is no evidence for specific effects of periodontal treatment procedures on increasing ischemic cardiovascular risk. Two observational studies reported no effect of invasive dental treatment in elevating ischemic cardiovascular risk [ ], and one study suggested a minimal increased risk within four weeks following treatment [ ]. Chen et al. [ ] performed a case-crossover and self-controlled case series using the Taiwanese National Health Insurance Research Database, including over 110,000 myocardial Infarction cases and 290,000 Ischemic Stroke patients, between 1999 and 2014. They reported a non-significant increase in the incidence of myocardial infarction within the first 24 weeks following invasive dental treatment (including periodontal procedures) except for a modest risk of myocardial infarction during the first week for patients without other comorbidities (OR = 1.31, 95% CI [1.08; 1.58], after 3 days). A registry-based case-control study between 2011 and 2013 including 51,880 cases who underwent an invasive dental procedure compared to 246,978 controls reported no association with increased incidence of myocardial infarction (OR 0.98, 95% CI [0.91; 1.06]) [ ]. Minassian et al. [ ] performed a self-controlled case series including nearly 10 million participants included in an insurance database from 2002 and 2006 in the USA. The analysis showed that invasive dental treatment (largely comprising of tooth extractions and only 4% being non-surgical and surgical periodontal procedures) is associated with an increased risk of incident acute cardiovascular events (IR = 1.5, 95% CI [1.09; 2.06]) within the first four weeks of treatment recorded. In summary, the Group concluded delivering periodontal treatment is safe with regard to cardiovascular risk. 5.1.2. What is the perioperative bleeding risk when performing periodontal therapy? Periodontal treatment consists of numerous procedures with different levels of bleeding risk. However, this risk of bleeding is low in the vast majority of procedures and can be easily controlled with local haemostatic measures. Perioperative bleeding risk varies according to the extent and invasiveness of the periodontal procedure performed. The majority of periodontal procedures may be grouped within the ESC/AHA/EHRA [ ]. Low Bleeding Risk (frequency less than 1% of post-operative bleeding) group: supragingival polishing, non-surgical periodontal treatment, conventional surgical periodontal treatment (conservative, resective or regenerative), tooth extractions and dental implant placement. Moderate bleeding risk (frequency between 2–5%) may be observed in major autogenous bone augmentation procedures, such as block bone harvesting, sinus floor elevation and procedures where healing is by secondary intention, such as free gingival grafting. In patients undergoing anti-platelet therapy Individuals undergoing single acetylsalicylic acid (ASA) therapy (aspirin) in different therapeutic dosages, as well as therapy with clopidogrel, ticlopidine or ticagrelor show no statistically significant differences in frequency of bleeding events when compared to controls (i.e., subjects not undergoing anti-platelet therapy) [ ]. Dual antiplatelet therapy, most commonly ASA in combination with clopidogrel, may pose a certain risk for postoperative bleeding complications; however, it appears these haemorrhagic events may be managed safely with local haemostatic measures [ ]. Thus, current evidence does not support discontinuation of antiplatelet therapy before dental procedures, irrespective of the type of therapy employed (single or dual antiplatelet therapy) or the type of procedure performed (single, multiple tooth extractions, non-surgical and surgical periodontal therapy and dental implant procedures). 5.2.2. In patients undergoing anti-coagulant therapy 5.2.2.1. Vitamin-K antagonists In patients taking oral anticoagulant therapy (vitamin-K antagonists, VKA) and undergoing dental extraction, minor dental procedures and dental implant placement do not seem to increase the risk of bleeding compared to patients who discontinue oral anticoagulant therapy [ ]. There may be a higher post-operative bleeding risk in patients continuing VKA and undergoing either minor dental surgery or other higher-risk procedures when compared to non-VKA patients [ ], but local haemostatic agents appear to be effective in controlling post-operative bleeding [ ]. 5.2.2.2. Novel/direct anticoagulants (DOAC/NOAC) Limited trials and evidence are available on the management of patients on novel oral anticoagulant (NOAC) therapy undergoing dental treatment; hence, the Group concluded further studies regarding dental procedures in these patients are strongly encouraged. It appears there is no need for interruption of NOAC therapy in most dental treatments due to a low incidence of bleeding complications, which can be successfully managed with local haemostatic measures when comparing groups continuing NOAC and groups discontinuing NOAC therapy [ , , , ], and with reported timing of discontinuation and reinstitution varying greatly. When comparing NOAC patients with healthy individuals, there seems to be a higher incidence of delayed bleeding (2 days and later) in those patients who do not discontinue NOAC therapy [ ]. 6. Collect a careful history to assess for CVD risk factors, such as diabetes, obesity, smoking, hypertension, hyperlipidemia and hyperglycemia. Suggestthe patient consults his/her physician if any of these risk factors are not appropriately controlled. Oral health education should be provided to all patients with periodontitis and a tailored oral hygiene regime, including twice-daily brushing, inter-dental cleaning and in some cases the use of adjunctive chemical plaque control may be appropriate. People presenting with a diagnosis of CVD should receive a thorough oral examination, which embeds a comprehensive periodontal evaluation, including full-mouth probing and bleeding scores. If no periodontitis is diagnosed initially, patients with CVD should be placed on a preventive care regime and monitored regularly (at least once a year) for changes in periodontal status. In people with CVD, if periodontitis is diagnosed, they should be managed as soon as their cardiovascular status permits. Irrespective of the level of CVD or specific medication, non-surgical periodontal therapy should be provided, preferably in several 30–45 minute sessions to minimize a spike of acute systemic inflammation Surgical periodontal and implant therapy, when indicated, should be provided in a similar manner as in patients without CVD. However, attention should be paid to: Hypertension. It is recommended to measure the patients’ blood pressure (after appropriate relaxation) before the surgical intervention, and in cases of high blood pressure (above 180/100 according to expert opinion), the surgery should be postponed until the patient’s blood pressure is stabilized. Medication with antiplatelet and anticoagulant drugs. Because periodontal and implant surgical procedures usually impart only a low to medium risk of bleeding in general terms, the dentist should not change a patient’s medication or in cases of doubt he/she should consult the physician/cardiologist prior to the surgical intervention. Consideration should also be given to the local management of bleeding complications that may arise. Current AHA/ACC/SCAI/ACS/ADA/ESC/ACCP guidelines on perioperative management of antithrombotic therapy do not suggest discontinuation of anti-platelet therapy for Low Bleeding Risk procedures [ , , ]. Various approaches for perioperative management of anticoagulant therapy have been suggested. The Group reviewed the guidelines on perioperative management of vitamin K antagonists (VKA) and suggests discontinuation of medication treatment if the INR is 4 or below for Low or Medium Bleeding Risk procedures [ ]. However, if the internationalised normalised ratio (INR) is 3.5 or above, the expert Group recommends dental clinicians seek advice and consult with the responsible medical professional. Management of high thromboembolic risk cases should be collaborative in consultation with the medical professional responsible for the VKA therapy [ ]. After reviewing novel anticoagulant (non VKA) and direct anticoagulant (NOAC/DOAC) therapies guidelines, the Group concluded that for Low Bleeding Risk periodontal procedures no discontinuation of anticoagulants is recommended [ ]. These procedures could be performed 18–24 hrs after the last intake (depending on a renal function assessment for the medication in question) and then restarted 6 hrs following treatment. The expert Group, however, strongly recommends the dental clinician consult with the responsible medical professional. When a Medium Bleeding Risk periodontal procedure is planned, discontinuation of therapy should be agreed with the medical professional responsible for and/or prescribing the anticoagulant therapy. Lastly, in cases of combined anti-platelet and anticoagulant therapies, which pertain to patients with the highest thrombotic and ischemic risk (i.e., chronic atrial fibrillation or after an acute myocardial infarction or recent coronary stenting), when periodontal procedures (either of Low or Medium Bleeding Risk) are required, any alterations in medication should be discussed and agreed upon with the responsible medical professional [ ]. In elective periodontal procedures, the operation should be delayed until after treatment stabilization and appropriate consultation with the medical specialist. If a positive diagnosis has been made, the physician should seek to ascertain that appropriate periodontal care and maintenance are being provided. Patients with CVD should be asked about any signs and symptoms of periodontitis, including bleeding gums during brushing or eating, loose teeth, spacing or spreading/drifting of the teeth, oral malodor and/or abscesses of the gums or gingival suppuration. If a positive history is elicited, then a prompt periodontal evaluation should be recommended before their scheduled annual check-up. In the case of a negative history, people with CVD should be advised to check for the above symptoms, and if a positive sign appears, they should visit their dentist at least once per year. For all patients with newly diagnosed CVD, referral for a periodontal examination should occur as part of their ongoing management of CVD. Even if no periodontitis is diagnosed initially, an annual oral/dental check-up is recommended. The physician should liaise with the dental surgeon over periodontitis management in CVD patients on anticoagulant/antiplatelet therapy prior to the oral intervention and/or periodontal surgery to avoid excess bleeding or the risk of ischaemic events. 6.3. Patients should inform their dentist about the outcome of their visits to the physician and provide an update on their CVD history and any changes in medications. Patients should inform the dentist if they are on anticoagulant therapy. Patients should understand it is important to keep their mouth and whole body as healthy as possible with regular dental and medical visits. 6.4. Your dentist will be able to pick up early signs of gum disease. 6.4.4. What can I do to prevent gum disease? You need to clean your teeth and gums twice daily at home for a minimum of two minutes. Also, cleaning between your teeth daily is important, and your oral health professional will show you how to do this. You should visit a dental surgeon as soon as possible for a diagnosis and advice on what you need to do. It is important to keep your mouth as healthy as possible with regular oral and dental care, according to the recommendations of your oral health professional. chunks.content: 1. Introduction Testicular cancer consists most often of seminomatous (60%) and non-seminomatous (40%) germ cell tumors (GCT). It is the malignancy with the highest incidence among patients aged 15–30 years [ ]. In most cases, the five-year survival for testicular GCTs is around 95%, owing to the integration of cisplatin-based chemotherapy in the therapeutic algorithm of both the metastatic and the localized disease. Overall and progression-free survival rates are inversely correlated with the disease stage and prognostic criteria according to the international germ cell collaborative consensus group. It is worthwhile mentioning that surgical orchiectomy remains the gold standard for the initial management of GCTs [ , , ]. Initial orchiectomy should be performed through an inguinal approach with the primary objective of preventing the lymphatic dissemination of CGTs, by preserving the integrity of the scrotal anatomy. In fact, peroperative scrotal violation was proven to be a significant risk factor for local recurrences. The latter are considered local when they occur in the scrotum and/or the inguinal area [ , ]. Even after an inguinal approach for testicular GCT orchiectomy, the medical literature reported few but very intriguing cases of local testicular GCT recurrences. Nonetheless, these were either a contiguous tumorous extension in a metastatic setting, or a delayed recurrence complicating violated tumors in the perioperative setting [ , ]. This is the reason why we deemed interesting the presentation of a case report discussing a local recurrence following an inguinal orchiectomy for a stage I, testicular mixed germ cell tumor GCT without tumor nor scrotal violation. 2. Case report We hereby report the case of a 40-year-old male, who works as a farmer in the North of France. His past medical and surgical history are mostly notable for a right undescended testis for which he underwent a scrotal right orchidopexy when he was 10 years old. Additional details concerning this specific intervention could not be retrieved due to the absence of a flagrant scar tissue and to the unawareness of the patient regarding the surgical approach. He was subsequently diagnosed many years later with a left testicular mixed GCT after a progressive increase in scrotal volume. A 6 × 5 cm left testicular tumor was confirmed upon ultrasound evaluation of the testis. His initial serum GCT markers were negative except for a serum alpha fetoprotein (AFP) level of 203.9 ng/ml. He underwent a left orchiectomy in October 2020, through an inguinal approach. The surgery was performed according to good practice guidelines, starting with the proximal ligation of the spermatic cord. No preoperative biopsy of the tumor was performed and no testicular prosthesis was left in place at the end of the procedure. Computed tomography (CT) of the chest, abdomen and pelvis was negative for secondary lesions. Pathology report showed a testicular GCT composed of 90% teratoma, <10% yolk sac tumor and <5% seminoma. His initial disease was stratified as a stage I (AJCC 2009 classification) pT1 (TNM 2017 classification) N0 M0 mixed GCT with predominant teratoma. Surgical margins were exempt from residual disease (R0) and the surgical specimen was not violated. However, a month later, in November 2020, his AFP levels remained elevated at 48.1 ng/ml. Therefore, his disease was restaged to Is, but he did not receive adjuvant therapy just yet. Instead, he underwent a CT surveillance of the abdomen and pelvis at 3, 6 and 13 months. In December 2021, he presented with a recurrence of his disease that was diagnosed on CT scan ( ) of the abdomen and pelvis, showing a 6 × 3.5 cm left external inguinal mass that proved to be mature teratoma when excised achieving an R0 status. Serum AFP levels dropped to 2.9 ng/ml. The latter episode was deemed to be a recurrence rather than a local progression due to the R0 status and moreover due to its exclusive implantation in the soft tissue, rendering it unbound to the lymphatic and vascular drainage of the testicle. No imaging was performed to evaluate the contralateral testis that was normal upon clinical evaluation. Four months later, in February 2022, he presented with another recurrence, this time taking the aspect of a 7.5 × 5.7 × 3.4 cm supra pubic palpable indurated nodule that was confirmed to be solitary on positron emission tomography (PET) computed tomography (PET CT) ( ). Tumor markers remained within normal range. The mass extended subcutaneously to the right inguinal area and came in close contact with the right inguinal cord and the aponeurosis of the right rectus abdominis muscle, that did not seem to be infiltrated by the tumor. Serum alpha-fetoprotein levels came back at 375 ng/ml. The excision of the aforementioned recurrence was rendered difficult due to its close contact with the right spermatic cord and its adhesion to soft tissues. However, excision was complete, and no tumor violation was recorded peroperatively. Histology report came in favor of a GCT with two tumorous clusters; a predominant post-pubertal teratoma (80%) and a less represented post-pubertal yolk sac cluster (20%). Nonetheless, the histological analysis was rendered challenging by the presence of a considerable cluster of smooth muscle cells, of “rhabdoïd” aspect, that could not rule a rhabdomyosarcoma (Immunohistochemistry was performed indeed to prove the SMC component but results were still doubtful as by our pathologist to rule out rhabdomyosarcoma). The AFP levels normalized in the postoperative course and the patient was scheduled to undergo adjuvant chemotherapy as per tumor board decision. 3. Discussion To our knowledge, this is only the second case reported in the medical literature, discussing soft tissue local recurrences following a complete (R0) excision of testicular mixed GCT through an inguinal approach without tumor violation. Our review consisted of a medline (pubmed) screening of the medical literature discussing local recurrences following inguinal orchiectomy for testicular GCTs. When orchiectomy was performed through an inguinal approach for a stage I mixed GCT, local recurrences only occurred when residual testis and/or tumor was left in place and an R0 status could not be reached. This was the case when a GCT in an undescended inguinal testicle was the differential diagnosis for a clinical inguinal hernia, diagnosed peroperatively. Pathology then failed to identify clear surgical margins, nor to individualize the epididymis, nor the spermatic cord, that were both resected after the patient developed a subsequent local recurrence [ ]. In fact, cryptorchidism constitutes a consensual risk factor for the development of testicular GCT and its treatment by scrotal orchidopexy presumes a previous opening of the various testicular tunicae to reach the tunica albuginea allowing for scrotal fixation through a scrotal counter incision. Therefore, the lymphatic drainage of the testicle has already been disrupted ever since its tunicae were explored [ ]. Moreover, the TNM classification of these patients should also be modified due to gonadal dysgenesis and dystrophy as well as the alteration of many surrounding tunicae. Our patient did not undergo a previous ipsilateral scrotal exploration- the orchidopexy was contralateral- and he still developed a local recurrence of his tumor despite a complete surgical excision. Furthermore, he also developed a soft tissue recurrence contralateral to the excised tumor. While analyzing the phenomenon of the malignant transformation in testicular teratoma (i.e. rhabdomyosarcoma), Azizi et al. [ ]. found that this can be due to the differentiation of a totipotent germ cell element into a somatic malignant cluster, and/or the presence of a 12p chromosome abnormality. They also suggested that pure mature teratoma found in metastatic residual sites after chemotherapy resulted from the selective destruction of non-teratomatous elements. Finally, they stated that teratomatous transformations almost always occurred in the testis first, explaining their presence in distant metastasis as well. In our case, the primary tumor did not contain immature teratoma nor somatic malignant transformations, unlike the recurrence in the right (i.e. contralateral) inguinal soft tissues. A literature review regarding local recurrences following inguinal orchiectomy for testicular GCTs points at the fact that these were always mixed GCT with a cluster of teratoma and the recurrence occurred early, within the first year after the primary orchiectomy. The local recurrence, however, always contained mature teratoma, either exclusively, or mixed with other GCT clusters [ , , ]. The local recurrence, however, always contained mature teratoma, either exclusively, or mixed with other GCT clusters [ , , ]. This was also the case of our patient for the ipsilateral recurrence, but not for the contralateral soft tissue masses where more immature tissue was found. The latter observation has never been reported in the medical literature so far. One problematic issue in patients with local recurrence is the proper classification of the recurring inguinal/soft tissue malignancy and thus the most appropriate therapeutic approach. As can be seen through the previously reported cases, including our patient, local recurrences after orchiectomy for a stage I primary testicular mixed GCT often presented with elevated serum biomarkers, which is normally a stigmata of metastatic disease stage Is. Vehawn et al. [ ], chose to treat the soft tissue inguinal recurrence by 3 cycles of bleomycin, etoposide and cisplatin (BEP) before removing the residual epididymis and spermatic cord. However, local recurrence still occurred within soft tissue ten months later, with no implication of inguinal lymph nodes, requiring an extensive soft tissue resection. Pathology showed soft tissue mature teratoma., known to be chemo resistant [ , ]. This approach follows the mainstay strategy inciting to treat metastatic NSGCT with initial chemotherapy, before surgically excising residual masses [ ]. Alternatively, when we opted for an initial surgical resection of local soft tissue recurrence at our facility, it was demonstrated through histological analysis that the recurrence was well circumscribed within soft tissue with predominant teratoma and a less expressed cluster of seminoma. However, five months later, local recurrence still occurred in the shape of a well circumscribed soft tissue mass with predominant teratoma as well. But, in the absence of chemotherapy in the therapeutic algorithm, serum tumor markers were supranormal at each recurrence and only normalized in the immediate postoperative course. In the absence of solid randomized controlled trials providing specific, overall and progression-free survival data, there is not enough evidence supporting an optimal therapeutic algorithm for the management of local mixed GCT recurrences following R0 inguinal orchiectomy. For instance, both surgery and chemotherapy, when used exclusively, failed to prevent the early relapse of a previously treated recurrence. Moreover, subsequent local relapse always occurred few months after the resection of the initial soft tissue recurrence. Thus, further research work is needed for more contributive conclusions regarding this rare and specific patient population in order to understand the etiology and the best therapeutic alternative of this specific patient population. When compared with data of the medical literature, the presence of immature tissue in the local recurrence may have caused earlier relapses but not necessarily worse prognosis. 4. Conclusion Mixed germ cell tumors can recur exclusively as soft tissue masses. These can occur even after achieving a R0 status according to good practice guidelines for primary orchiectomy. Immature tissue can be found when they are resected.

chunks.content: Introduction Periodontitis is a chronic, microbial biofilm-induced inflammatory disease that progressively damages the tooth-supporting tissues. Periodontitis is among the most prevalent oral diseases globally with significant public health concerns, especially due to its impact on systemic health and overall quality of life of people. According to the Global Burden of Disease Report in 2021, 12.5% of the world’s population is affected with severe periodontitis. WHO Global Oral Health Status Report (GOHSR-2019) also reveals that the global prevalence of periodontitis is approximately 19% among individuals aged over 15 years, accounting for more than one billion cases worldwide. Microbial biofilm is the primary cause of periodontitis, which progresses from reversible gingivitis to destructive disease affecting the periodontal ligament, cementum, and alveolar bone. While tissue destruction typically corresponds to biofilm accumulation, progression is heavily influenced by host defences and risk factors like diabetes and smoking, making a patient’s risk profile crucial in current classifications. Periodontitis is site-specific, characterised by uneven attachment and bone loss throughout the dentition, rather than uniform destruction. The primary aim of periodontal treatment is to establish a stable oral environment, enabling patients to maintain health through effective self-care. Consequently, the patient’s periodontal care pathway must integrate prevention, timely diagnosis, intervention, and long-term maintenance. As current scientific evidence confirms that periodontitis is largely preventable and manageable, clinical approaches must bridge both preventive and curative strategies. This paper critically traces the shifting paradigms of periodontitis management from the past to contemporary clinical practice, highlighting how these evolving frameworks have reshaped clinical decision-making and improved patient care. Methods This structured review synthesises evolving concepts and guidelines for managing periodontitis. While not a formal systematic review, it incorporates minimal PRISMA‑ScR elements to ensure transparency and reproducibility ( ). • Databases searched: PubMed/MEDLINE and Scopus. • Date range: Period covering the transition from previous classifications to contemporary stage/grade frameworks. • Search strategy: Boolean strings combining MeSH terms and keywords. For example: ("Periodontitis"[MeSH] OR "periodontal disease") AND ("classification" OR "management" OR "guidelines" OR "therapy" OR "concepts"). • Language limits: English-language only. • Inclusion criteria: Peer‑reviewed articles, systematic reviews, consensus statements, and guideline documents relevant to classification and management of periodontitis. • Exclusion criteria: Case reports, editorials, non‑peer‑reviewed sources, and studies not directly addressing management paradigms. • Study types retained: Systematic reviews, narrative reviews, consensus guidelines, and landmark clinical studies. Shifting paradigms in aetiology and pathogenic progression Microbial aetiology and dysbiosis While microbial biofilm is the established aetiology of periodontal disease (PDD), the understanding of its pathogenic progression has evolved significantly since the 19th century. Walter Loesche’s Specific Plaque Hypothesis (1976) proposed that disease results from specific, pathogenic microorganisms within the complex oral flora, rather than the total plaque mass. Consequently, Porphyromonas gingivalis , Prevotella intermedia , Tannerella forsythia , Aggregatibacter actinomycetemcomitan s, and spirochetes such as Treponema denticola were identified as key periodontal pathogens, distinct from the Streptococcus and lactobacilli species associated with dental caries. Alternatively, the nonspecific plaque hypothesis (NSPH) emerged, proposing that PDD stems from total microbial biomass rather than specific pathogens, as similar bacteria are found in both health and disease. However, long-term studies questioning the NSPH revealed that individual susceptibility, rather than merely bacteria, determines attachment loss, highlighting varying disease rates even without toothbrushing, which shifted the focus of PDD aetiology toward host response and risk factors. As conceptual understanding shifted, the Ecological Plaque Hypothesis (EPH) emerged, suggesting that environmental stressors disrupt the balance of oral microbiota, favouring the proliferation of pathogenic species. Building on this, Socransky et al categorised periodontal bacteria into colour-coded complexes based on their association with health and disease. The pathogenic mechanisms and disease progression models are illustrated in . Further advancing this field, Hajishengallis and colleagues introduced the 'Keystone Pathogen Hypothesis,' which proposes that low abundances of Porphyromonas gingivalis can disproportionately influence the host immune response, leading to dysbiosis and disease progression. Microbial dysbiosis is driven by inflammation, which alters the local environment, promoting the growth of pathogenic species. This has led to a paradigm shift in the understanding of periodontitis, that while the aetiology remains microbial, its pathogenesis is strongly influenced by inflammatory processes. Since the commensal microbiome is resilient and cannot be eradicated, treatments should combine biofilm disruption and risk factor control as the foundation of care, with inflammation-modulating strategies acting to be complementary rather than substitutive. With evolving concepts, a new unifying hypothesis, Inflammation-Mediated Polymicrobial-Emergence and Dysbiotic-Exacerbation (IMPEDE) Model was proposed. IMPEDE complements the current classification of periodontal diseases developed by the AAP & EFP, which views periodontitis as a chronic inflammatory disease due to dysbiotic biofilm. This linear model (continuous model) is aligned with the traditional view that disease progression is a steady, predictable process. Contrary to this older model, modern evidence suggests
